pages.name: Count it with bars
pages.text: A gas held at one temperature keeps `pV` the same: Boyle's law, which is `pV^n = C` with `n = 1`, the [[isothermal]] case. This one starts at 400 kPa in 0.1 m³, so `C = 400 × 0.1 = 40` kJ, and its pressure falls along `p = 40 ÷ V`. The work it does is the area under that curve, but both old rules divide by 0 here. So count the area with bars, as in Calculus fundamentals, and watch their total settle as they thin.
pages.alt: A graph of pressure against volume, with the curve p equals 40 divided by V, from 0.1 to 0.2 cubic metres. Key: pV equals 40. Key: bars: their total is the work.

pages.name: Why no rule?
pages.task: Why can't the reverse power rule find the area under `p = 40 ÷ V`?
pages.answer: Its power is −1, and adding one gives 0, so it would divide by 0
pages.why: `40 ÷ V` is `40 × V^−1`. The reverse power rule adds one to the power, giving `V^0`, then divides by the new power, 0, which cannot be done. The area itself is fine: the bars stop at V₂ and settle on 27.73 kJ, and the curve bends, since `p` halves each time `V` doubles.
pages.alt: A graph of pressure against volume, with the curve p equals 40 divided by V, from 0.1 to 0.2 cubic metres. Key: pV equals 40. Key: 0.1 to 0.2 cubic metres: 27.73 kJ.

pages.name: The next doubling
pages.task: From 0.1 to 0.2 m³ the bars total 27.73 kJ. What do the bars from 0.2 to 0.4 m³ total?
pages.why: From 0.2 to 0.4 m³ the stretch is twice as long, so each bar is twice as wide, and at twice the volume `40 ÷ V` is half the pressure, so each bar is half as tall. Twice the width times half the height is the same area, so the total is 27.73 kJ again.
pages.alt: A graph of pressure against volume, with the curve p equals 40 divided by V, from 0.1 to 0.2 cubic metres. Key: pV equals 40. Key: 0.1 to 0.2 cubic metres: 27.73 kJ. Key: 0.2 to 0.4 cubic metres: 27.73 kJ.

pages.name: Double it
pages.text: Here is why. Two bars from 0.1 to 0.2 m³ stand beside two from 0.2 to 0.4 m³. Each bar on the right is twice as wide, because its stretch is twice as long, and half as tall, because at twice the volume `40 ÷ V` is half the pressure. Cut one in two and lay it over its partner: the same area. So every doubling holds the same work, wherever it starts. Double it puts V₂ at twice V₁; drag either handle to start anywhere.
pages.alt: A graph of pressure against volume, with the curve p equals 40 divided by V, from 0.1 to 0.4 cubic metres. Key: pV equals 40. Key: bars: their total is the work.

pages.name: From 0.1 to 0.8
pages.task: What work does the gas do expanding from 0.1 to 0.8 m³?
pages.why: Only the ratio counts: `0.8 ÷ 0.1 = 8 = 2 × 2 × 2`, three doublings, each holding 27.73 kJ, so `3 × 27.73 = 83.18` kJ. Seven steps of 0.1 m³ are equal gaps, not equal ratios: the later steps are at lower pressure and hold less. And 8 is the ratio, not the number of doublings.
pages.alt: A graph of pressure against volume, with the curve p equals 40 divided by V, from 0.1 to 0.8 cubic metres. Key: pV equals 40. Key: 0.1 to 0.2 cubic metres: 27.73 kJ. Key: 0.1 to 0.8 cubic metres: 83.18 kJ.

pages.name: The stretch that adds C
pages.text: Which stretch adds exactly C? Cut the volume from 0.1 m³ into `k` bars, each one part in `k` of the volume where it starts wide, and as tall as the curve at its left edge. Each holds `40 ÷ k`, so the `k` bars make 40 kJ every time, and the last ends at `(1 + 1/k)^k × 0.1`, lesson 2's sum, which settles on e × 0.1. The bars stand a little above the curve, by less as they thin, so the area from V₁ to e × V₁ is exactly C. Each further stretch by e adds another C, so the work is C times the number of e-stretches from V₁ to V₂, and that number is the power of e that makes V₂ ÷ V₁, lesson 4's power you need: `ln(V₂ ÷ V₁)`. So `W = C × ln(V₂ ÷ V₁)`. Check it with one part: that bar ends at 0.2 m³, and `40 × ln 2 ≈ 40 × 0.693 = 27.73` kJ, the hundred bars' total on screen 1.
pages.alt: A graph of pressure against volume, with the curve p equals 40 divided by V. Key: pV equals 40. Key: bars, each 40 divided by k kJ. A dashed line marks e times 0.1, about 0.272 cubic metres.

pages.name: From 0.1 to 0.3
pages.task: What work does the gas do expanding from 0.1 to 0.3 m³?
pages.why: `V₂ ÷ V₁ = 0.3 ÷ 0.1 = 3`, and ln 3 is about 1.099, so `W = 40 × ln 3 ≈ 43.94` kJ. The log key gives `40 × log 3 ≈ 19.08`, counting ten-fold stretches, not e-fold ones. And `0.3 − 0.1 = 0.2` is the difference: `40 × ln 0.2` is about −64.38, minus, though the gas expands.
pages.alt: A graph of pressure against volume, with the curve p equals 40 divided by V, from 0.1 to 0.3 cubic metres. Key: pV equals 40. Key: 0.1 to 0.3 cubic metres: 43.94 kJ.

pages.name: Squeeze it
pages.text: Now run it the other way. Squeeze it swaps the handles: a piston pushes the gas from 0.2 m³ back to 0.1 m³, and its pressure climbs from 200 to 400 kPa. Every change in volume is now minus, so each bar's width is minus: the bars are hatched and both readouts turn minus. `V₂ ÷ V₁ = 0.5`, the same as 200 ÷ 400, and a ratio below 1 has a minus ln. The gas does minus work, which means the piston does that much work on it.
pages.alt: A graph of pressure against volume, with the curve p equals 40 divided by V, from 0.1 to 0.2 cubic metres, squeezed. Key: pV equals 40. Key: bars: their total is the work. Key: hatched: squeezed, so minus.

pages.name: Squeezed from 0.4
pages.task: A piston squeezes the gas from 0.4 m³ to 0.1 m³. What work does the gas do?
pages.why: `V₂ ÷ V₁ = 0.1 ÷ 0.4 = 0.25`, a ratio below 1, so its ln is minus: `40 × ln 0.25 ≈ −55.45` kJ, two halvings of −27.73 kJ each. The gas does −55.45 kJ of work, so the piston does 55.45 kJ on it. `pV` is 40 at both ends, but the work is the area under the curve, not the change in `pV`.
pages.alt: A graph of pressure against volume, with the curve p equals 40 divided by V, from 0.1 to 0.4 cubic metres, squeezed. Key: pV equals 40. Key: squeezed, 0.4 to 0.1 cubic metres: minus 55.45 kJ.

pages.name: Show n = 1.3
pages.text: Show n = 1.3 lays a second gas from the same start, one where `p × V^1.3` stays the same, a [[polytropic]] process as in Calculus fundamentals, with 1.3 an example value. The pressure axis stretches to 800 kPa so its curve fits. Here `pV` is a fixed number ÷ `V^0.3`, which shrinks as the gas expands, so this curve falls below the steady one: 162 kPa at 0.2 m³, against 200. Its work, from `(p₁V₁ − p₂V₂) ÷ (n − 1)`, is the third readout.
pages.alt: A graph of pressure against volume, with the curve p equals 40 divided by V, from 0.1 to 0.2 cubic metres. Key: pV equals 40. Key: bars: their total is the work. Key: the n equals 1.3 curve. Key: the area under it. A second curve shows the n equals 1.3 gas from the same start.

pages.name: Which takes less work?
pages.task: Squeezed from 0.2 m³ at 200 kPa to the same end volume, 0.1 m³, which gas takes less work?
pages.why: Squeezed, the n = 1.3 gas's `pV`, a fixed number ÷ `V^0.3`, grows as `V` shrinks, so its curve climbs to 492 kPa, above the steady 400, and holds more area: 30.82 kJ against 27.73. Expanding, it gave less work, but squeezing runs its `pV` the other way. Both end at 0.1 m³, but the work is the area under the path, not set by its ends. That is for the same end volume: squeezed to the same end pressure instead, the n = 1.3 gas would stop short of 0.1 m³.
pages.alt: A graph of pressure against volume, with the curve p equals 40 divided by V, from 0.1 to 0.2 cubic metres, squeezed. Key: pV equals 40. Key: the steady squeeze. Key: the n equals 1.3 curve. Key: the area under it. A second curve shows the n equals 1.3 gas from the same start.

pages.name: A gas at 300 kPa
pages.task: A gas at 300 kPa in 0.1 m³ expands at a steady temperature to 0.5 m³. What work does it do?
pages.why: `C = p₁V₁ = 300 × 0.1 = 30` kJ, and `V₂ ÷ V₁ = 0.5 ÷ 0.1 = 5`. ln 5 is about 1.609, so `W = 30 × ln 5 ≈ 48.28` kJ. `30 × log 5 ≈ 20.97` uses the log key, which counts ten-fold stretches, and `300 × ln 5` leaves V₁ out of C.
pages.alt: A graph of pressure against volume, with the curve p equals 30 divided by V, from 0.1 to 0.5 cubic metres. Key: the gas: pV the same. Key: 0.1 to 0.5 cubic metres: 48.28 kJ.

pages.name: The compressor
pages.task: Say an air compressor squeezes 0.08 m³ of air at 100 kPa to 800 kPa, at a steady temperature. What work does the air do?
pages.why: `C = 100 × 0.08 = 8` kJ. `pV` stays at 8, so the air ends at `8 ÷ 800 = 0.01` m³, and `V₂ ÷ V₁ = 1/8`, the same as `100 ÷ 800`. ln(1/8) is about −2.079, so `W = 8 × ln(1/8) ≈ −16.64` kJ: the air does −16.64 kJ of work, so the piston does 16.64 kJ on it. The log key gives −7.22, counting ten-fold stretches.
pages.alt: A graph of pressure against volume, with the curve p equals 8 divided by V, from 0.01 to 0.08 cubic metres, squeezed. Key: the air: pV the same. Key: the squeeze: minus 16.64 kJ.

pages.name: A preview: ln x
pages.text: A preview of where this leads. Here is `y = 1 ÷ x`, the same curve with `C = 1`, shaded from 1 to `x`. With `C = 1` and `V₁ = 1`, the area `C × ln(x ÷ 1)` is just `ln x`. Drag `x` along. One more thin strip, `h` wide, at `x` adds about `h × 1 ÷ x`, so `ln x` climbs at a rate of `1 ÷ x`: the slope of `ln x` is `1 ÷ x`. The Derivatives course takes this up.
